question: Has India really ended poverty? What the World Bank's 2026 report shows, and why economists still argue

parts.title: Out of the pit
parts.at: Has India really ended extreme poverty?

parts.title: Not out of the woods
parts.at: If almost nobody is that poor, why does it feel like most people are still struggling?

parts.title: Working, and still poor
parts.at: Poor Indians work as many hours as anyone else. Why are they still poor?

parts.title: Why nobody agrees on the number
parts.at: Why doesn't India have an official poverty line any more?

parts.title: What the spending numbers cannot see
parts.at: Is being above the line the same as being well?

keyNumbers.label: Indians below the World Bank's extreme poverty line, about Rs 68 a day, in 2024
Indians below the World Bank's line for upper-middle-income countries, about Rs 187 a day
of all the world's people below that higher line live in India
real growth in a farm labourer's daily wage, 2014-15 to 2024-25, against 62% for GDP per person

visualPlan.title: Almost no Indian is below the lowest poverty line now. Four in five are below the higher one
visualPlan.subtitle: Share of Indians below each World Bank line, 1990-2030 · price-adjusted (PPP) dollars a person a day, 2021 prices · dots are survey years; after 2024 the lines are estimates
visualPlan.why: The whole answer in one picture: the lowest line has almost emptied, the highest has not.
visualPlan.read: Each line is the share of Indians below one poverty line. The lower the line, the faster it fell.
visualPlan.watch: After 2024 the lines are estimates from growth forecasts, not new surveys.

visualPlan.title: The world's fall in extreme poverty stalled after 2019. India's kept going
visualPlan.subtitle: Share of people below $3 a day (2021 PPP dollars), 1990-2026 · World Bank estimates; 2025-26 are estimates, and India's 2015-21 values are filled in without survey data
visualPlan.why: Places India's fall against a world where progress has stopped.
visualPlan.read: India started above the world average and is now far below it; the world line has been flat since about 2019.
visualPlan.watch: India has no usable survey for 2015-21, so those years are the World Bank's estimates.

visualPlan.title: India has 18% of the world's people, 4% of its extremely poor, and 30% of everyone below $8.30
visualPlan.subtitle: India's share of the world's poor at each World Bank line in 2024, beside its share of world population · 2021 PPP dollars

columns.label: India's share of the world's poor

visualPlan.why: Shows why India drops out of the extreme-poverty story and becomes the centre of the wider one.
visualPlan.read: Compare the two bars in each row. Where India's share of the poor is above its share of people, India is over-represented.
visualPlan.watch: The poverty shares are for 2024 and the population share for 2026.

visualPlan.title: A 10% fall in spending would push the share of Indians below $4.20 a day from 15% to 23%
visualPlan.subtitle: Share of Indians below each line in 2024, and after a hypothetical 10% fall in everyone's spending · 2021 PPP dollars
visualPlan.why: Shows how many people sit just above each line.
visualPlan.read: The gap between the two dots is the number of people within 10% of the line.
visualPlan.watch: A thought experiment, not a forecast.

visualPlan.title: 47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.20 a day. In Goa, under 3% do
visualPlan.subtitle: Share of people below $4.20 a day (about Rs 95) by state and union territory · World Bank subnational atlas, 2023 reference year, from HCES 2023-24
visualPlan.why: Shows where the poor are concentrated.
visualPlan.read: Darker states have a larger share of people below $4.20 a day.
visualPlan.watch: Small states and union territories rest on small samples.

visualPlan.title: In every state, small children are more likely than the average resident to live in a poor household
visualPlan.subtitle: Share below $8.30 a day, children aged 0-5 against everyone, 14 selected states · World Bank state estimates from the 2023-24 household survey
visualPlan.why: Poverty falls hardest on households with young children.
visualPlan.read: In every row the child dot sits to the right of the everyone dot.
visualPlan.watch: This measures the household's spending per person, not what each child eats.

visualPlan.title: India has less extreme poverty than Bangladesh or Indonesia, but more people below $8.30
visualPlan.subtitle: Share of people below each line in 2024 · 2021 PPP dollars · Indonesia from a 2024 survey, the others are estimates
visualPlan.why: Tests India's record against its neighbours at every line.
visualPlan.read: Compare each country across the three lines.
visualPlan.watch: A selection of Asian countries, not a ranking.

visualPlan.title: Poor Indians work almost the same hours as everyone else
visualPlan.subtitle: Average weekly hours of people in work, by household above or below $3 a day · India, 2024 · World Bank
visualPlan.why: Rules out laziness or idleness as the explanation.
visualPlan.read: The two dots in each row are close together.
visualPlan.watch: Hours, not pay. This uses the $3 line.

visualPlan.pairWith: Poor Indians work almost the same hours as everyone else
visualPlan.title: Poor workers are more often self-employed and on farms
visualPlan.subtitle: Share of workers, by household above or below $8.30 a day · India, 2024 · World Bank
visualPlan.why: What differs is the kind of work, not the amount.
visualPlan.read: Poor workers' dots sit further right on both rows.
visualPlan.watch: This uses the $8.30 line, unlike the hours chart beside it.

visualPlan.title: Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has grown 62%. A farm labourer's real wage has grown 9%
visualPlan.subtitle: Real GDP per person and real daily wages, 2014-15 = 100 · rural wages for men (Labour Bureau, CPI-Rural), factory wage per day worked (Annual Survey of Industries, CPI-Combined) · rural 2019-20 and 2020-21 incomplete
visualPlan.why: Tests whether growth reached the pay of the people most likely to be poor.
visualPlan.read: Every line starts at 100 in 2014-15. GDP per person climbs; the wage lines stay near 100.
visualPlan.watch: Wage rates for men, not household income. Women's wages and days of work are not shown.

visualPlan.title: If poor households had better-off households' jobs and pay, the share below $8.30 would fall from 79% to 57%
visualPlan.subtitle: World Bank simulation for India, 2024 · share of people below each line and how far below it they are, now and simulated
visualPlan.unit: % of population or of the line
visualPlan.why: Sizes the jobs route out of poverty.
visualPlan.read: Compare the two bars in each row.
visualPlan.watch: An accounting exercise, not a forecast or a policy.

visualPlan.title: New price data raised India's extreme poverty rate and lowered its $4.20 rate, from the same survey
visualPlan.subtitle: India's 2023-24 poverty rates under the World Bank's old (2017) and new (2021) price base · same survey, same release
visualPlan.why: Shows that a change of yardstick moved the numbers, not a change in people's lives.
visualPlan.read: Each row is one line. The dots show the same survey measured two ways.
visualPlan.watch: The dollar values of the lines differ between the two price bases.

visualPlan.title: Depending on the line and the method, India's 2022-23 poverty rate is anywhere from 2% to 26%
visualPlan.subtitle: Published estimates for 2022-23 · World Bank (direct survey) and Himanshu, Lanjouw and Schirmer (2025, bridging old and new surveys)
visualPlan.why: Shows how much of the argument is about the line and the method.
visualPlan.read: Each bar is one published estimate. Compare bars that use the same line.
visualPlan.watch: The spread mixes different lines and methods; it is not a margin of error.

visualPlan.title: Between the two newest surveys, the poorest tenth's spending grew fastest
visualPlan.subtitle: Change in average real spending by tenth of the population, HCES 2022-23 to 2023-24 · World Bank
visualPlan.why: Shows who gained within the two comparable surveys.
visualPlan.read: Each bar is one tenth of the population, poorest at the top.
visualPlan.watch: Different households in each survey; the survey misses many of the richest.

visualPlan.title: Since 1977, household spending in the national accounts has more than quadrupled. In the surveys, it has only doubled
visualPlan.subtitle: Real GDP per person, household spending in the national accounts, and average spending in the household surveys, 1977 = 100 · World Bank · grey links join surveys that are not comparable
visualPlan.why: Shows the gap behind the argument that surveys miss the rich.
visualPlan.read: All three start at 100 in 1977. The survey line rises least.
visualPlan.watch: The gap has several causes; this chart cannot split them.

visualPlan.title: Money poverty is the smallest of these numbers
visualPlan.subtitle: Six measures, each with its own population and year · child stunting NFHS-5 (2019-21), health-spending hardship (2022), World Bank measures from HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24
visualPlan.why: Shows what a spending line cannot see.
visualPlan.read: Each bar is a separate measure. They overlap and cannot be added.
visualPlan.watch: Different years and populations: stunting is of children under five.

sourceNotesExtra.label: RBI Database on Indian Economy, Average Daily Wage Rates in Rural India for Men (Labour Bureau, report 664): all-India rates by occupation, 2014-15 to 2024-25, used for the wage index.
sourceNotesExtra.manual: DBIE is a client-rendered app; the report was exported through its public guest access on 2026-10-08 and is frozen with its hash in data/raw/poverty-debate-wages-2026-11/.

sourceNotesExtra.label: RBI Database on Indian Economy, Annual Survey of Industries principal characteristics (report 155): wages to workers and days worked, 2014-15 to 2023-24.
sourceNotesExtra.manual: DBIE is a client-rendered app; the report was exported through its public guest access on 2026-10-08 and is frozen with its hash in data/raw/poverty-debate-wages-2026-11/.

sourceNotesExtra.label: MoSPI, Consumer Price Index (2012=100), rural and combined, monthly: deflators for the wage index and the Tendulkar comparison.
MoSPI, National Accounts Statistics: real GDP per person at 2011-12 prices.
Press Information Bureau, 11 January 2023: free foodgrain under the National Food Security Act from 1 January 2023 for more than 80 crore people.
Press Information Bureau, 29 November 2023: Cabinet extends free foodgrain (PMGKAY) to about 81.35 crore beneficiaries for five years from 1 January 2024.
World Bank, Global Poverty Monitoring Technical Note 44 (June 2025): India's welfare aggregate, valuation of free ration grain, single national PPP.
World Bank, India poverty methodology note (2025): the switch of 2011-12 estimates from URP to MMRP and spatial price deflation.
World Bank, PIP methodology handbook, welfare aggregate: India's 2011-12 rate under URP (22.9%) and MMRP (16.2%), 2017 PPPs.
Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, World Inequality Lab Working Paper 2024/09: top 1% income share 22.6% and wealth share 40.1% in 2022-23.
MoSPI, NSS Report 592, Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023-24: coverage exclusions and the Census 2011 rural sampling frame.

furtherReading.label: Himanshu, Peter Lanjouw and Philipp Schirmer (2025), Tinbergen Institute Discussion Paper TI 2025-069/V. The most careful attempt to bridge the 2011-12 and 2022-23 surveys; puts 2022-23 poverty between about 11% and 26% depending on the line.

Surjit Bhalla, Karan Bhasin and Arvind Virmani (2022), IMF Working Paper WP/22/69, Pandemic, Poverty, and Inequality: Evidence from India. The case that extreme poverty had all but ended by 2019 once free food is counted.
World Bank (2025), India poverty methodology note. How the World Bank builds India's numbers from the new surveys: recall period, free grain, price adjustments.
C. Rangarajan and S. Mahendra Dev, Counting the Poor (MSE Monograph 30). The reasoning behind the higher 2014 line that was never adopted.
Arindam Das and Jean Drèze (2024), The problem of India's stagnant real wages, Ideas for India. A decade of rural wages, and why they matter for the poverty debate.

Nitin Kumar Bharti, Lucas Chancel, Thomas Piketty and Anmol Somanchi (2024), Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922-2023: The Rise of the Billionaire Raj. Inequality from income and wealth data, not spending surveys.
NITI Aayog (2024), Multidimensional Poverty in India since 2005-06. The government's count of poverty beyond spending.
